subject: math
title: Multiplication to Three Digits
seo_title: Grade 5 Multiplication Worksheets: Area Models and the Standard Algorithm (Free, BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Multiplication and division to three digits, including division with remainders
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 math worksheets on multiplication for the BC curriculum: facts to 100, multiplying by 10 and 100, area models, the standard algorithm (2-digit × 2-digit and 3-digit × 1-digit) and BC word problems. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Split the numbers by place value and multiply every part. In the standard algorithm, the tens row starts with a zero.
body_html:
Start with the facts

Every big multiplication is built from facts to 10 × 10. If a fact is slow, use one you know: 7 × 8 is 7 × 7 = 49 plus one more 7, so 56. Division facts come from the same family: 56 ÷ 8 = 7.

Multiply by 10, 100 and multiples of 10

× 10 moves every digit one place to the left: 34 × 10 = 340. × 100 moves every digit two places: 34 × 100 = 3400.

For 20 × 30, use 2 × 3 = 6. Tens × tens = hundreds, so 20 × 30 = 600. For 47 × 60, find 47 × 6 = 282, then write one 0: 2820.

The area model

Split each number into tens and ones. Draw a rectangle with one part for each pair. Multiply each part, then add all the parts.

A 3-digit number makes three parts: hundreds, tens and ones.

The standard algorithm

For 3-digit × 1-digit, start with the ones. Write the ones digit of each product and regroup the tens into the next column. Multiply first, then add the regrouped digit.

For 2-digit × 2-digit, make one row for each digit of the bottom number. Row 1 multiplies by the ones digit. Row 2 multiplies by the tens digit, so it starts with a placeholder zero (green). Then add the two rows.

Each row of the algorithm is one row of the area model. For 24 × 13, row 1 is 24 × 3 = 72 (the 3 row: 60 + 12). Row 2 is 24 × 10 = 240 (the 10 row: 200 + 40). 72 + 240 = 312, the same answer.

Estimate to check

Is 38 × 24 = 912 reasonable?

Round to the nearest ten: 40 × 20 = 800. 912 is close to 800, so it makes sense. An answer like 228 or 9120 is far off.

Answer: Yes

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Forgetting the zero in the tens row (38 × 24 = 152 + 76 = 228)Row 2 is × 20, so write 0 first: 760
20 × 30 = 60Tens × tens = hundreds: 20 × 30 = 600
Only two parts (24 × 13 = 200 + 12)There are four parts: 200 + 40 + 60 + 12 = 312
Not adding a regrouped digit (236 × 4 = 824)Write it small and add it: 3 × 4 + 2 = 14
Adding the regrouped digit firstMultiply first, then add: 3 × 4 + 2 = 14, not (3 + 2) × 4

faq.q: What multiplication do Grade 5 students learn in the BC math curriculum?
faq.a: The Grade 5 BC curriculum lists multiplication and division to three digits, plus multiplication and division facts to 100. Students practise questions such as 24 × 13 and 236 × 4 with area models and the standard algorithm.

faq.q: How do you teach 2-digit by 2-digit multiplication?
faq.a: Start with the area model: split both numbers into tens and ones and add the four parts, so 24 × 13 = 200 + 40 + 60 + 12 = 312. Then show the standard algorithm, where each row is one row of the area model.

faq.q: Why do you put a zero in the second row?
faq.a: The second row multiplies by the tens digit. In 38 × 24 the 2 means 2 tens, so the row is 38 × 20 = 760, not 38 × 2 = 76. The zero keeps the digits in the right places.

faq.q: Do Grade 5 students in BC still need to know their times tables?
faq.a: Yes. Multiplication and division facts to 100 are part of the Grade 5 BC curriculum, and quick recall makes 2- and 3-digit multiplication much easier.

items.q: An orchard in the Okanagan packs 48 apples in each box. How many apples are in 26 boxes?
items.e: 26 boxes × 48 apples, so multiply 48 × 26. Row 1: 48 × 6 = 288. Row 2: 48 × 20 = 960 (write the placeholder 0, then 48 × 2 = 96). Add: 288 + 960 = 1248.

items.q: A SkyTrain carries 145 riders on one trip. How many riders does it carry on 8 trips?
items.e: 8 trips × 145 riders, so multiply 145 × 8. 5 × 8 = 40, write 0, regroup 4; 4 × 8 + 4 = 36, write 6, regroup 3; 1 × 8 + 3 = 11, write 11. Answer: 1160 riders.

items.q: Each tray at the school bake sale holds 36 cookies. The Grade 5 class fills 18 trays. How many cookies is that?
items.e: 18 trays × 36 cookies, so multiply 36 × 18. Row 1: 36 × 8 = 288. Row 2: 36 × 10 = 360 (write the placeholder 0, then 36 × 1 = 36). Add: 288 + 360 = 648.

items.q: A lacrosse club in Burnaby buys 16 new sticks for $34 each. How much does the club spend?
items.e: 16 sticks × $34, so multiply 34 × 16. Row 1: 34 × 6 = 204. Row 2: 34 × 10 = 340 (write the placeholder 0, then 34 × 1 = 34). Add: 204 + 340 = 544.

items.q: Which is the best estimate for 67 × 48?
items.e: Round each number to the nearest ten. 67 has 7 ones, so it rounds up to 70. 48 has 8 ones, so it rounds up to 50. 70 × 50 = 3500 (tens × tens = hundreds). The exact answer is 3216, close to 3500.

items.q: A school garden in Surrey is 23 m long and 14 m wide. What is its area?
items.e: Area = 23 m × 14 m, so multiply 23 × 14. Row 1: 23 × 4 = 92. Row 2: 23 × 10 = 230 (write the placeholder 0, then 23 × 1 = 23). Add: 92 + 230 = 322.

items.q: A BC Ferries ship carries 236 cars on each sailing. How many cars do 6 sailings carry?
items.e: 6 sailings × 236 cars, so multiply 236 × 6. 6 × 6 = 36, write 6, regroup 3; 3 × 6 + 3 = 21, write 1, regroup 2; 2 × 6 + 2 = 14, write 14. Answer: 1416 cars.

items.e: 28 days × 35 minutes, so multiply 35 × 28. Row 1: 35 × 8 = 280. Row 2: 35 × 20 = 700 (write the placeholder 0, then 35 × 2 = 70). Add: 280 + 700 = 980.

items.q: Simran's class takes part in the Terry Fox Run. Each of the 27 students raises $35. How much does the class raise?
items.e: 27 students × $35, so multiply 35 × 27. Row 1: 35 × 7 = 245. Row 2: 35 × 20 = 700 (write the placeholder 0, then 35 × 2 = 70). Add: 245 + 700 = 945.

items.q: Jasleen works out 72 × 39 = 2808. Estimate to check. Is her answer reasonable?
items.e: Estimate: 72 × 39 is about 70 × 40 = 2800. 2808 is close to 2800, so the answer is reasonable.

items.q: Volunteers plant cedar seedlings in 37 rows, with 24 seedlings in each row. How many seedlings do they plant?
items.e: 37 rows × 24 seedlings, so multiply 24 × 37. Row 1: 24 × 7 = 168. Row 2: 24 × 30 = 720 (write the placeholder 0, then 24 × 3 = 72). Add: 168 + 720 = 888.

items.q: A group snowboard lesson costs $45 for each student. 23 students from Harjot's school sign up. What is the total cost?
items.e: 23 students × $45, so multiply 45 × 23. Row 1: 45 × 3 = 135. Row 2: 45 × 20 = 900 (write the placeholder 0, then 45 × 2 = 90). Add: 135 + 900 = 1035.

items.q: Which is the best estimate for 86 × 29?
items.e: Round each number to the nearest ten. 86 has 6 ones, so it rounds up to 90. 29 has 9 ones, so it rounds up to 30. 90 × 30 = 2700 (tens × tens = hundreds). The exact answer is 2494, close to 2700.

items.q: Each shelf in the school library holds 128 books. How many books fit on 7 shelves?
items.e: 7 shelves × 128 books, so multiply 128 × 7. 8 × 7 = 56, write 6, regroup 5; 2 × 7 + 5 = 19, write 9, regroup 1; 1 × 7 + 1 = 8, write 8. Answer: 896 books.

items.q: A hockey team in Kelowna orders hoodies that cost $42 each. What is the best estimate of the cost of 19 hoodies?
items.e: Round 19 to 20 and $42 to $40. 20 × $40 = $800. The exact cost is 19 × $42 = $798, very close. (Rounding $42 up to $50 gives $1000, which is too far off.)

items.q: Liam works out 58 × 34 = 406. Estimate to check. Is his answer reasonable?
items.e: Estimate: 58 × 34 is about 60 × 30 = 1800. 406 is far from 1800, so it cannot be right. Liam forgot the placeholder 0 in the tens row. The correct answer is 1972.

items.q: 4 classes in Nanaimo each raise 175 salmon eggs in a classroom tank. How many eggs is that in all?
items.e: 4 classes × 175 eggs, so multiply 175 × 4. 5 × 4 = 20, write 0, regroup 2; 7 × 4 + 2 = 30, write 0, regroup 3; 1 × 4 + 3 = 7, write 7. Answer: 700 eggs.

items.q: The hockey arena in Kamloops has 24 rows of seats with 38 seats in each row. How many seats are there?
items.e: 24 rows × 38 seats, so multiply 38 × 24. Row 1: 38 × 4 = 152. Row 2: 38 × 20 = 760 (write the placeholder 0, then 38 × 2 = 76). Add: 152 + 760 = 912.
